name: net
doc:
Addresses on a network, as the data they are.

An IPv4 address is four octets, an IPv6 address eight hextets, a port a number under 65536, a domain a list of labels. Every platform holds each of these as a type of its own and writes it as text, and every platform's parser and printer settle the corners a little differently: leading zeros, uppercase hex, where `::` goes, whether an IPv4-mapped address is written with dots. Saying the type once, as bounded numbers, puts validity in the type — `[256, 1, 1, 1]` is refused by the checker, with no parser involved — and leaves the text as what it is: two propositions, parsing and printing, proved on each platform and held to one answer.

types.name: octet
types.doc: One byte of an IPv4 address. Rust spells this `u8`.

types.name: hextet
types.doc: One sixteen-bit group of an IPv6 address. Rust spells this `u16`.

types.name: IpV4
types.doc: An IPv4 address: four octets, in network order, so `[1, 2, 3, 4]` is 1.2.3.4. Rust spells this `[u8; 4]`, which is what `Ipv4Addr::from` takes and `octets()` gives back.

types.name: IpV6
types.doc: An IPv6 address: eight hextets, in network order, so `::1` is seven zeros and a one. Rust spells this `[u16; 8]`, which is what `Ipv6Addr::from` takes and `segments()` gives back.

types.name: IpAddr
types.doc: Either kind of address, tagged, since four numbers and eight numbers are both lists and a value would not otherwise say which it is.

types.name: label
types.doc: One label of a domain name: one to sixty-three bytes. A label on the wire is ASCII — punycode for anything else — so its scalar values and its bytes are the same count, and both are bounded so that neither reading of `length` lets a long one through.

types.name: Domain
types.doc: A domain name as its labels, lowercase: `example.com` is `["example", "com"]`. A whole name is at most 253 bytes, which no bound on a list of labels can say; a proof of a parser is where that would be held.

types.name: Host
types.doc: What a URL's host is: a name to resolve, or an address to connect to.

types.name: Scheme
types.doc: The two schemes a website answers to.

types.name: Origin
types.doc: Where a website is: a scheme, a host, and a port when it is not the scheme's own.

functions.name: parse_v4
functions.doc:
The address a dotted quad spells, or nothing if the text is not one.

Four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 joined by dots, and nothing else: no leading zeros, because `01.2.3.4` has been read as octal by some platforms and as decimal by others, and an address that two platforms read differently is not an address; no spaces, no port, no prefix length, no hexadecimal.

functions.name: format_v4
functions.doc: An address as a dotted quad, which has only one spelling.

functions.name: parse_v6
functions.doc:
The address IPv6 text spells, or nothing if it is not one.

The text of RFC 4291: up to eight groups of one to four hexadecimal digits in either case, one `::` standing for a run of one or more zero groups, and the last two groups allowed to be a dotted quad. Nothing else: no zone (`fe80::1%eth0`), no brackets, no port, no prefix length. Every platform's parser accepts all of the former; they part ways on the latter, which is why it is said here.

functions.name: format_v6
functions.doc: An address as RFC 5952 says to write it, which is the one spelling every reader agrees on: lowercase hexadecimal, no leading zeros in a group, `::` for the longest run of two or more zero groups and for the first such run when two are as long, a lone zero group left as `0`, and an IPv4-mapped address (`::ffff:0:0/96`) with its last four bytes as a dotted quad — which the RFC recommends, and which not every platform's printer does.
